title: Preach the Word, Finish the Course
summary: Paul solemnly charges Timothy to preach the word, testifies to his finished course and coming crown, and closes with personal requests and greetings.
historicalContext: Paul writes from a Roman prison during what appears to be a second captivity, some years after the house arrest described at the close of Acts. Conditions are harsher now. Onesiphorus had to search the city to find him (1:16–17), most of his co-workers have scattered, and at the first hearing of his case no advocate stood with him. He no longer weighs release against death as he did in Philippians; he expects execution under Nero, probably in the mid-sixties of the first century. Winter is approaching, when shipping on the Mediterranean would close, so his requests for Timothy to come quickly carry real urgency. Timothy is still laboring in Ephesus, and Tychicus is being sent to take his place. The names in this chapter trace the network of the Pauline mission across Asia, Macedonia, Achaia, Dalmatia, and Rome, and they show an aged apostle arranging the work he must leave behind.
literaryContext: This chapter brings the letter to its climax and close. The solemn charge of verses 1–5 gathers the earlier commands—stir up the gift, guard the deposit, endure hardship, rightly divide the word, continue in the Scriptures—into nine imperatives that open with “preach the word” and end with “make full proof of thy ministry.” Paul then grounds the charge in his own testimony (vv. 6–8): Timothy must carry on because the apostle is being poured out. Christ’s appearing frames the section (vv. 1, 8), and his kingdom reappears in the doxology of verse 18. The personal notes of verses 9–18 are bracketed by two urgent requests to come and set faithful companions against deserters and an opponent. Throughout, “the Lord” is the steady center (vv. 8, 14, 17, 18, 22). Greetings and a twofold benediction bring the apostle’s last known letter to its end.
themes: The charge to preach the word in every season
Sound doctrine and the appetite for pleasing myths
A finished course and a crown kept for Christ’s appearing
Faithfulness and desertion among fellow workers
The Lord who stands by his servants
Grace for the church after the apostle’s departure

outline.title: The Final Charge to Timothy
outline.summary: Before God and the coming Judge, Paul charges Timothy to preach the word with patience, resist the drift toward myths, and fulfill his ministry.

outline.title: Poured Out and Awaiting the Crown
outline.summary: Paul describes his approaching death as a drink offering and a departure, reviews his finished course, and looks to the crown given at Christ’s appearing.

outline.title: Companions, Deserters, and a Warning
outline.summary: Paul urges Timothy to come, reports who has left and who remains, requests his cloak and scrolls, and warns against Alexander.

outline.title: The Lord Who Stood By Him
outline.summary: Forsaken by all at his first defense, Paul was strengthened by the Lord to proclaim the message and trusts him for final deliverance into the heavenly kingdom.

outline.title: Greetings and Grace
outline.summary: Paul sends greetings, reports on Erastus and Trophimus, repeats his plea to come before winter, and closes with a blessing for Timothy and the church.

verses.bibleText: I charge thee therefore before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, who shall judge the quick and the dead at his appearing and his kingdom;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
With “I charge thee therefore” Paul begins the last and most solemn appeal of the letter. He has just described the God-breathed Scriptures that equip the man of God for every good work (3:16–17), and now he places Timothy under oath to use them. The charge is made “before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ.” Timothy serves in the presence of the Father and the Son, who see every motive and every word.

Paul then names Christ in his role as the one “who shall judge the quick and the dead.” “Quick” is the older English word for living. The phrase gathers the whole human race into one tribunal: those still alive when Christ returns and those who have died before it. The dead do not face that judgment as souls already sorted into their destinies; they are summoned from the grave by the voice of the returning Lord (John 5:28–29; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). The verdict of the righteous Judge is fixed to a day in the future, and every minister’s work will be weighed then.

“At his appearing and his kingdom” is best understood as part of the oath itself: Paul adjures Timothy by Christ’s appearing and by his reign. The appearing is the visible, personal return of Christ in glory, and the kingdom is the everlasting dominion he will establish when he comes (Daniel 7:14, 27; Matthew 25:31). Paul will return to both, speaking of the crown given to those who love “his appearing” (v. 8) and of being preserved for “his heavenly kingdom” (v. 18).

The force of the charge lies in its perspective. A preacher who forgets the coming Judge will be tempted to measure success by applause or numbers. One who remembers him will speak with courage and with care, knowing that both the messenger and the hearers must give account to the same Lord.

wordNotes.term: διαμαρτύρομαι (diamartyromai) — I charge
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to testify solemnly or to adjure, calling witnesses to confirm a weighty obligation. Paul uses it for formal commands given in God’s presence, and the first person singular carries his apostolic authority. It turns the instruction that follows into a sworn trust.

wordNotes.term: ἐπιφάνεια (epiphaneia) — appearing
wordNotes.explanation: The word denotes a visible manifestation, often used of a ruler’s arrival or a deity’s self-disclosure. In 2 Timothy 1:10 it refers to Christ’s first coming; here, as in verse 8, it points to his glorious return, an event as public and personal as his coming in the flesh.

verses.bibleText: Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The content of the charge opens with three words: “Preach the word.” The verb belongs to the world of the herald, the official who announced a ruler’s decree publicly and without alteration. A herald does not invent the message; his task is to deliver it clearly and faithfully. “The word” is the message from God that Paul has already called “the word of God” and “the word of truth” (2:9, 15), the gospel rooted in the Scriptures that have shaped Timothy since childhood (3:15). The command excludes speculation, entertainment, and human opinion offered in place of revelation. Jesus kept to truths that met his hearers’ daily needs, and his servants follow that pattern.

“Be instant in season, out of season” calls for readiness at every moment. The verb pictures someone standing at his post, on duty and alert. The paired adverbs play on the idea of a fitting time: Timothy must preach whether the occasion seems favorable or unfavorable. The inconvenience may be on the side of the hearers, who are not in the mood to listen, or on the side of the preacher, whose natural reserve might counsel silence (1:7). Neither condition releases him from the charge.

Three further imperatives describe how the word is applied. To “reprove” is to bring a wrong into the light and show it to be wrong, convincing the conscience with evidence from Scripture. To “rebuke” is to censure and call a harmful course to a halt. To “exhort” is to urge and encourage, coming alongside those who need strength to obey. Ministry that only comforts or only condemns distorts the word.

All of this is to be done “with all longsuffering and doctrine.” Patience governs the manner and teaching governs the method. Correction without patience hardens people and dishonors Christ, who bears long with sinners. Correction without instruction may stop a behavior for a moment while leaving the false belief that produced it in place. Timothy must be persistent and gentle, firm and explanatory, because the goal is restoration to the truth (2:24–26).

wordNotes.term: κήρυξον τὸν λόγον (kēryxon ton logon) — preach the word
wordNotes.explanation: The imperative comes from the verb for a herald’s public proclamation. Its decisive aorist form gives the command urgency. “The word” needs no qualifier because the letter has already identified it as God’s message of truth, so the herald’s authority rests entirely on the message he did not compose.

wordNotes.term: εὐκαίρως ἀκαίρως (eukairōs akairōs) — in season, out of season
wordNotes.explanation: The two adverbs form a wordplay on καιρός, a fitting time: “when it is opportune and when it is not.” The phrase does not commend tactlessness. It insists that the preacher’s faithfulness is not controlled by convenience, his own or his hearers’.

verses.bibleText: For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“For the time will come” gives the reason the charge cannot wait. Paul has just told Timothy to preach out of season, and now he describes that unfavorable season. The warning stands in line with others he had given about a coming falling away within the church itself (Acts 20:29–30; 2 Thessalonians 2:3; 1 Timothy 4:1). Such conditions were already beginning in Ephesus, but the prophecy reaches beyond Timothy’s day and describes a recurring tendency that would intensify as the end approaches.

The people Paul describes are not outsiders hostile to the faith. They are hearers who once sat under the truth but will no longer “endure sound doctrine.” The verb means to bear with or listen willingly. Healthy teaching makes demands; it exposes sin, calls for repentance, and reorders life around God’s will. Those who find this intolerable do not abandon religion; “after their own lusts” they “heap to themselves teachers.” The verb pictures piling up an assortment of instructors, chosen by one standard: whether they satisfy what the hearers already want. The listeners have made themselves the measure of truth.

The “itching ears” belong to the hearers, as the Greek construction makes plain. They crave novelty and the pleasant sensation of messages that stimulate without penetrating. Their appetite creates the market; the trouble begins in the audience.

This verse calls every believer to examine his own listening. It is possible to prefer teachers because they confirm our desires, to collect voices that never trouble the conscience, and to call that spiritual growth. The remedy is a love for the truth that welcomes correction (2 Thessalonians 2:10).

wordNotes.term: κνηθόμενοι τὴν ἀκοήν (knēthomenoi tēn akoēn) — having itching ears
wordNotes.explanation: The participle describes feeling an itch, and “hearing” stands for the ear itself. The image is of curiosity seeking constant stimulation, relieved only by whatever is new or flattering. The participle agrees with the hearers, so the craving lies in the audience who seek out the teachers.

wordNotes.term: ὑγιαινούσης διδασκαλίας (hygiainousēs didaskalias) — sound doctrine
wordNotes.explanation: “Sound” means healthy, using the language of physical wellbeing. Teaching that agrees with the gospel nourishes spiritual health and produces godly living, while false teaching spreads like disease (2:17). The phrase is characteristic of the Pastoral Letters.

verses.bibleText: And they shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Verse 4 completes the portrait with two movements. First, “they shall turn away their ears from the truth.” The verb implies a prior relationship; these are people who once professed to hold the truth and now deliberately avert their hearing from it. The refusal is a choice. No one is driven from the truth by divine decree; the hearers decide what they will listen to and so shape their own course.

Second, they “shall be turned unto fables.” A different verb is used, one that describes swerving off a path. The passive form suggests that once the ear is closed to truth, people are carried aside almost without noticing. Turning from the truth never leaves a neutral space. Something always fills the vacancy, and here it is “fables,” myths that have the appeal of religion without its reality.

In the Pastoral Letters these myths seem to have included speculative tales and genealogies drawn from Jewish lore and elaborated by the false teachers (1 Timothy 1:4; Titus 1:14). Their danger was that they could be dressed in biblical language. Texts torn from their setting can be made to support what the Bible never teaches. The contrast Paul draws is between “the truth,” God’s message grounded in what he has done in Christ, and stories that lack historical and spiritual substance (2 Peter 1:16).

The progression is sobering: refusing sound teaching, gathering agreeable teachers, closing the ear, drifting into myth. Each step seems small. The safeguard is a heart that keeps returning to the word itself and remains willing to hear what it does not prefer.

wordNotes.term: μύθους (mythous) — fables
wordNotes.explanation: In the New Testament a mythos is a story lacking truth or historical reality, set against the factual gospel. The definite article here may point to the particular myths circulating among the Ephesian false teachers, though the warning applies to every substitute for revealed truth.

wordNotes.term: ἐκτραπήσονται (ektrapēsontai) — shall be turned
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to turn aside or wander from a course. Paul uses it of those who swerved from love and a good conscience into empty talk (1 Timothy 1:6) and of widows who turned aside after Satan. It describes a drift away from the right road rather than a single dramatic break.

verses.bibleText: But watch thou in all things, endure afflictions, do the work of an evangelist, make full proof of thy ministry.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But watch thou” turns sharply back to Timothy. The Greek places an emphatic “you” at the head of the sentence, setting him against the restless hearers and their teachers. While others drift toward whatever pleases them, Timothy must be different.

The verb translated “watch” means to be sober. In the New Testament it is used figuratively for a mind free from every kind of spiritual intoxication, clear, steady, and alert, especially in view of Christ’s return (1 Thessalonians 5:6–8; 1 Peter 4:7). Timothy is to keep this composure “in all things,” in every circumstance and under every pressure. False teaching often thrives on excitement and novelty; the servant of Christ answers with calm judgment.

“Endure afflictions” repeats a theme that runs through the letter. Paul has already called Timothy to share in hardship as a good soldier (1:8; 2:3), and he has described his own sufferings for the gospel (2:9). Faithful ministry will not shield him from difficulty; it will often bring it.

“Do the work of an evangelist” reminds Timothy that settled pastoral responsibility in Ephesus does not cancel the task of proclaiming the gospel to those who have not believed. The title is used of Philip, whose ministry in Acts 8 consisted of announcing Jesus so that people would believe and be baptized. Whatever his role in the church, Timothy must keep announcing the good news.

Finally, “make full proof of thy ministry” gathers all the preceding commands into one. The verb means to fill up or bring to complete fulfillment. Timothy’s service must leave nothing undone. In verse 2 and here together Paul has issued nine imperatives, beginning with “preach the word” and ending with this summary. The next verse explains why the charge is pressing: the apostle who trained Timothy is about to be poured out, and the younger man must carry the work forward.

wordNotes.term: νῆφε ἐν πᾶσιν (nēphe en pasin) — watch thou in all things
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to be sober, used figuratively of clear-headed self-control and spiritual alertness. Its present tense, standing among aorist commands, suggests a continuing disposition required in every situation. Elsewhere it is linked with readiness for the Lord’s coming.

wordNotes.term: τὴν διακονίαν σου πληροφόρησον (tēn diakonian sou plērophorēson) — make full proof of thy ministry
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to fulfill completely or carry through to the end. Diakonia is service, the task Christ has assigned. Paul asks Timothy to carry out the whole range of that service, just as he would say the proclamation had been fully accomplished through him (v. 17).

verses.bibleText: For I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“For I” stands in deliberate contrast with the “but thou” of verse 5. Timothy must carry the ministry forward because Paul’s own part in it is ending. The apostle does not lament his situation or plead for sympathy. He interprets his approaching death in the language of worship.

“I am now ready to be offered” renders a single verb that means to be poured out as a drink offering. Under the sanctuary system a measure of wine was poured out with the burnt offerings and other sacrifices (Numbers 15:5–10; 28:7). Writing to the Philippians, Paul had spoken of this as a possibility (Philippians 2:17); now it is underway. The present tense, joined with “now” (literally “already”), shows that the outcome is settled even though a little time remains, enough for Timothy to make the journey and bring the cloak and scrolls (vv. 9, 13). The apostle’s blood, shed in martyrdom, would complete a life already given to God as an offering.

“The time of my departure is at hand.” The noun for departure describes a loosing, the word used for slipping a ship’s mooring lines or taking down a tent when an army breaks camp. Paul is speaking plainly about his death, and the verb “is at hand” means that the hour has arrived or stands immediately before him.

The image of departure should be read with the rest of Paul’s teaching about death. He consistently describes those who die in Christ as sleeping until the Lord returns and raises them (1 Thessalonians 4:13–16; 1 Corinthians 15:51–52). His departure is a release from the labors and chains of this life, a rest in the grave in the keeping of God, not the flight of a conscious soul into heaven. That is why the very next words look beyond death to “that day,” the day of Christ’s appearing, when the crown laid up for him will be given (v. 8). For the one who sleeps in Jesus, the next moment of awareness will be the resurrection morning.

wordNotes.term: σπένδομαι (spendomai) — I am ready to be offered
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to pour out a libation, the drink offering that accompanied sacrifices in Israel’s worship. Its present tense and passive voice present Paul’s death as already in motion and as something done to him, yet he sees it as an act of devotion to God.

wordNotes.term: ἀνάλυσις (analysis) — departure
wordNotes.explanation: Found only here in the New Testament, the noun means a loosing or unfastening, as of a vessel released from its moorings or a camp struck for travel. It is a gentle figure for death, consistent with Paul’s description of the faithful dead as those who sleep until the resurrection.

verses.bibleText: I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul now looks back over his ministry in three short clauses, each built the same way: the object placed first for emphasis, then a verb in the perfect tense. The perfect describes completed action with lasting result. At the end of his life these things stand established.

“I have fought a good fight” is literally “I have contested the good contest.” The noun can describe an athletic competition or a military struggle; Paul uses both images elsewhere, and the emphasis falls on strenuous, sustained effort. The contest is “good” because it is undertaken for God and for the gospel. He now testifies that he has done what he urged Timothy to do (1 Timothy 6:12; 2:3).

“I have finished my course” uses the language of the racetrack. At Miletus, years before, Paul had told the Ephesian elders that he did not count his life dear so that he might finish his course with joy (Acts 20:24). That hope has been realized. He does not claim to have won the race, only to have run the course God assigned him to its end without turning aside.

“I have kept the faith” can be read in more than one way. It may mean that Paul has continued believing, that he has guarded the truth entrusted to him unaltered, or that he has kept his pledge like a loyal soldier. In a letter so concerned with guarding the deposit (1:14) and resisting those who turn from the truth (4:3–4), the second sense is prominent, yet it includes the first: one cannot preserve the faith for others while abandoning it oneself.

These words are not a boast. Paul has said repeatedly that whatever he accomplished was the work of grace (1 Corinthians 15:10; 1 Timothy 1:12–14), and in this very chapter he will testify that the Lord stood by him and strengthened him (v. 17). He speaks so that Timothy will see that a life of faithful endurance is possible for anyone who relies on the same grace.

wordNotes.term: τὸν καλὸν ἀγῶνα ἠγώνισμαι (ton kalon agōna ēgōnismai) — I have fought a good fight
wordNotes.explanation: The cognate noun and verb describe a contest or struggle, at home both in athletics and warfare. The article marks it as the particular contest of faith in which all believers are engaged. The perfect tense views Paul’s entire ministry as a completed struggle.

wordNotes.term: τὴν πίστιν τετήρηκα (tēn pistin tetērēka) — I have kept the faith
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to guard, preserve, or keep watch over. With “the faith” it describes both personal perseverance and faithful custody of the gospel’s content. The same concern appears in Paul’s command to guard the good deposit committed to Timothy.

verses.bibleText: Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day: and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Having looked back, Paul now looks ahead. “Henceforth” translates a word meaning “for the rest” or “what remains.” His fighting, running, and keeping are finished; what remains is the reward. “There is laid up for me a crown of righteousness.” The verb means stored away, set aside and held in safekeeping. Paul’s crown already exists in God’s purpose, and nothing the Roman court does can touch it.

The crown is the victor’s wreath awarded at the games, the image Paul used when he contrasted the perishable garland of the athlete with the imperishable crown of the believer (1 Corinthians 9:25). It is called a crown “of righteousness.” The phrase may mean the crown that consists in righteousness, the perfected state of right standing and right character that the redeemed will enjoy, or the crown appropriate to one who has lived righteously. Either way, it does not rest on human merit. The righteousness Paul sought was the righteousness that comes through faith in Christ (Philippians 3:9), and the crown is a gift of grace from the Lord who made him righteous.

It will be given by “the Lord, the righteous judge.” Paul faced an earthly judge whose verdict could be unjust. Above that tribunal sits the Judge whose decisions are always right, and he will reverse every wrong verdict passed on his servants.

The timing is decisive: “at that day.” In this letter “that day” is the day of Christ’s appearing (1:12, 18; 4:1). Paul does not expect to be crowned at the moment of execution. His death will be a departure into rest, and the crown will wait in God’s keeping until the Lord returns, raises the dead, and rewards his people (Revelation 22:12). The next clause confirms this: the crown is given “not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing.” The apostle and the humblest believer, those who died centuries apart and those alive at Christ’s return, will receive their reward together on the same day (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; Hebrews 11:39–40).

Those who receive it are described as people who “love his appearing.” The perfect tense pictures a settled love that has shaped their whole lives. Such love is more than a doctrine about the second advent. It orders a whole life around the Lord’s coming and moves the believer to purify himself as Christ is pure (1 John 3:2–3). Two verses later Paul will name a man who loved the present world instead.

wordNotes.term: ὁ τῆς δικαιοσύνης στέφανος (ho tēs dikaiosynēs stephanos) — a crown of righteousness
wordNotes.explanation: The stephanos was the wreath given to a victor or honored citizen, distinct from a royal diadem. Similar phrases such as “crown of life” and “crown of glory” describe the reward itself. Here righteousness is the reward, given by grace through Christ and conferred at his coming.

wordNotes.term: τοῖς ἠγαπηκόσι τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν αὐτοῦ (tois ēgapēkosi tēn epiphaneian autou) — them that love his appearing
wordNotes.explanation: The perfect participle describes those who have loved, and continue to love, Christ’s visible return. The same verb appears in verse 10 for Demas, who loved the present age. What a person loves determines the direction of his life and the hope he holds.

verses.bibleText: Do thy diligence to come shortly unto me:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The letter turns abruptly from the crown to a personal request: “Do thy diligence to come shortly unto me.” The verb means to make every effort or to hurry, and “shortly” adds urgency. In verse 21 Paul will repeat the plea with a deadline: “before winter.”

The request does not contradict the calm certainty of verses 6–8. Roman legal proceedings could take months, and Paul expects some time to remain, enough for Tychicus to carry the letter to Ephesus and for Timothy to travel to Rome. But he writes as a man who knows the end will come soon, and he wants his spiritual son beside him before it does.

The longing is human and honorable. Strong faith in the coming crown does not erase the desire for a friend’s presence. Jesus himself, on the night before his death, asked his disciples to stay and watch with him (Matthew 26:38). The gospel never treats the need for companionship as weakness, and Paul’s request invites Timothy to share in the final stage of his master’s ministry.

wordNotes.term: σπούδασον ἐλθεῖν (spoudason elthein) — do thy diligence to come
wordNotes.explanation: The imperative means to make haste or exert every effort. Paul uses the same verb when he urges Timothy to study to show himself approved (2:15) and when he asks Titus to come to him at Nicopolis. Here it conveys both urgency and affection.

verses.bibleText: For Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world, and is departed unto Thessalonica; Crescens to Galatia, Titus unto Dalmatia.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul explains why he needs Timothy: his circle of helpers has dwindled. He begins with the most painful case. “Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world.” Demas had been a trusted co-worker. During the first imprisonment he was with Paul in Rome and joined in greetings to Colossae and to Philemon (Colossians 4:14; Philemon 1:24). Now he has left the apostle in the hour of greatest need.

The verb for “forsaken” means to abandon or leave someone in the lurch, the same word Paul uses in verse 16 for those who deserted him at his trial. Paul states the motive plainly: Demas “loved this present world,” or more literally, “the present age.” The phrase deliberately recalls verse 8. The faithful love Christ’s appearing; Demas loved the age that is passing away. The danger of the moment, the shame attached to a condemned prisoner, or the pull of comfort and safety proved stronger than his loyalty. Scripture does not tell us whether he later returned, and readers should be cautious about pronouncing on his final destiny. His story stands as a warning that years of service do not make a believer immune to the attraction of the world (1 John 2:15–17).

Demas went to Thessalonica, perhaps his home. The other names that follow do not carry the same reproach. Crescens, mentioned nowhere else, has gone to Galatia, and some manuscripts read Gaul. Titus, Paul’s trusted delegate in Corinth and Crete, has gone to Dalmatia, a region on the eastern coast of the Adriatic, north of Nicopolis where Paul had once asked to meet him (Titus 3:12). These men were apparently sent on assignments of ministry, and their absence reflects the continuing advance of the gospel even while its leading apostle sat in chains.

The contrast is instructive. Two men left Paul’s side for the sake of the mission; one left for the sake of himself.

wordNotes.term: ἀγαπήσας τὸν νῦν αἰῶνα (agapēsas ton nyn aiōna) — having loved this present world
wordNotes.explanation: Aiōn denotes the world viewed as an age, the present order that stands opposed to the age to come. Paul uses “this present age” for the realm of values Christians must not be conformed to. The verb echoes verse 8, setting love for the present age against love for Christ’s appearing.

wordNotes.term: ἐγκατέλιπεν (enkatelipen) — hath forsaken
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to leave behind, desert, or abandon someone in trouble. It appears in the cry of Psalm 22:1 quoted by Jesus on the cross, and in Paul’s assurance that persecuted believers are never forsaken by God.

verses.bibleText: Only Luke is with me. Take Mark, and bring him with thee: for he is profitable to me for the ministry.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Only Luke is with me.” Of all Paul’s fellow workers, only the physician remains at his side. Luke had shared many of Paul’s journeys, including the dangerous voyage to Rome, as the “we” passages in Acts reveal (Acts 27:1–2; 28:16). Paul once called him “the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14). He stayed in a city where friendship with Paul had become hazardous, a loyalty that sought no recognition.

Paul then asks Timothy, “Take Mark, and bring him with thee: for he is profitable to me for the ministry.” The request carries a story of failure and restoration. Years earlier John Mark had left Paul and Barnabas partway through their first missionary journey (Acts 13:13). When Barnabas wanted to take him again, Paul refused so firmly that the two missionaries parted company (Acts 15:37–39). Yet Mark did not remain defined by that failure. He later appears with Paul during the first Roman imprisonment, named as a fellow worker (Colossians 4:10; Philemon 1:24), and he was closely associated with Peter (1 Peter 5:13).

Now the apostle who once judged Mark unfit for the work asks specifically for him and calls him “profitable,” useful for service. Paul held no grudge, and Mark had grown into the kind of worker who could be trusted in a crisis.

The verse offers hope to anyone who has faltered in God’s service. Failure need not be final. Grace restores, and a worker who once turned back can become indispensable. It also challenges those who lead: Paul was willing to revise his judgment and welcome the one he had once refused.

wordNotes.term: εὔχρηστος (euchrēstos) — profitable
wordNotes.explanation: The adjective means useful or serviceable. Paul uses it of a vessel fit for the master’s use and of Onesimus, who had once been useless but was now useful. Applied to Mark, it marks the transformation of a once-failed helper into a valued servant of the gospel.

wordNotes.term: εἰς διακονίαν (eis diakonian) — for the ministry
wordNotes.explanation: Diakonia is service, the same word Paul used for Timothy’s ministry in verse 5. It probably refers to gospel work in Rome rather than mere personal attendance, though the two need not be separated. Mark is wanted as a partner in the ministry Paul still carries on.

verses.bibleText: And Tychicus have I sent to Ephesus.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Tychicus have I sent to Ephesus.” Tychicus was a believer from the province of Asia who had traveled with Paul on the journey that carried the collection to Jerusalem (Acts 20:4). During the first Roman imprisonment he delivered the letters to the Ephesians and the Colossians, and Paul called him a beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord (Ephesians 6:21–22; Colossians 4:7–8).

The verb may be read as “I am sending,” written from the standpoint of the recipient who will read the letter after Tychicus has arrived. If so, Tychicus probably carried this letter himself. His mission explains why Paul can ask Timothy to leave: Tychicus will take up the work in Ephesus so that the church is not left without oversight while Timothy and Mark travel to Rome. Paul had made a similar arrangement for Crete (Titus 3:12).

Even as he faces death, the apostle plans for the welfare of the congregations. His concern for “all the churches” (2 Corinthians 11:28) did not end when his own ministry was closing.

wordNotes.term: ἀπέστειλα (apesteila) — have I sent
wordNotes.explanation: The aorist of the verb meaning to send on a mission may be an epistolary aorist, describing an action as past from the reader’s perspective though present to the writer. Read this way, Paul is dispatching Tychicus with the letter, probably to replace Timothy at Ephesus.

verses.bibleText: The cloke that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Few verses in Paul’s letters are as ordinary, and few reveal the man so vividly. “The cloke that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring with thee.” The garment was a heavy outer cloak, a large circular piece of thick material with an opening for the head, worn for protection against cold and rain. With winter approaching (v. 21) and a damp Roman cell around him, Paul needed it. He had left it at Troas, a port on the route from Asia to Macedonia, in the home of Carpus, a believer mentioned only here.

Paul also asks for “the books, but especially the parchments.” The books were scrolls, ordinarily made of papyrus. The parchments were made of prepared animal skin, a more durable and costly material used for writings of special value. Their contents are not stated. They may have included portions of the Scriptures, Paul’s own notes, or documents useful for his defense. The phrase can also be read as “the books, that is, the parchments,” making the second term a clarification of the first.

Whatever they were, the request shows that the apostle remained a student to the end. Facing execution, he still wanted to read, study, and work. The man who had just written of his crown also felt the cold and asked for a coat. Faith does not make believers indifferent to bodily needs, and caring for those needs is part of loving one another.

wordNotes.term: φαιλόνης (phailonēs) — cloke
wordNotes.explanation: Found only here in the New Testament, the word corresponds to the Latin paenula, a heavy sleeveless travel cloak that covered the body against wind and rain. Its mention reflects the approach of winter and the hardship of Paul’s imprisonment.

wordNotes.term: τὰ βιβλία, μάλιστα τὰς μεμβράνας (ta biblia, malista tas membranas) — the books, but especially the parchments
wordNotes.explanation: Biblia are scrolls or written documents; membranai are parchment sheets or notebooks, a Latin loanword. Malista usually means “especially,” though it can mean “that is.” The request shows Paul’s continuing devotion to study and to the written word.

verses.bibleText: Alexander the coppersmith did me much evil: the Lord reward him according to his works:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul turns from his needs to a danger. “Alexander the coppersmith did me much evil.” The name was common, and the title “coppersmith” was used for metalworkers of every kind. This may be the Alexander whom Paul had earlier delivered to Satan for blasphemy (1 Timothy 1:20), or the Alexander pushed forward during the riot at Ephesus (Acts 19:33–34), but certainty is not possible. Timothy evidently knew whom Paul meant.

The verb translated “did” literally means “showed” or “displayed,” and in legal settings it could describe informing against someone. Alexander may have brought charges that led to Paul’s arrest or testified against him at his hearing. The harm he did seems to have been aimed at Paul’s message and defense rather than his body (v. 15).

“The Lord reward him according to his works.” The words echo a principle that runs through Scripture: God renders to every person according to what he has done (Psalm 62:12; Proverbs 24:12; Romans 2:6). Many manuscripts read the verb as a future statement, “the Lord will reward him,” which expresses confidence in God’s justice rather than a wish for revenge. Either way, Paul does not retaliate or plot his own vindication. He leaves the matter with the righteous Judge (Romans 12:19), the same Lord who will give the crown of righteousness at his appearing (v. 8).

The verse shows how a servant of God can name a wrong honestly without being consumed by bitterness. Justice belongs to the Lord, and entrusting it to him frees the wronged person to continue in faithfulness.

wordNotes.term: χαλκεύς (chalkeus) — coppersmith
wordNotes.explanation: Originally a worker in copper or bronze, the term came to denote any smith or metalworker. It identifies Alexander by trade, distinguishing him from others of the same common name. Ephesus, with its trade in silver shrines, had a strong guild of such craftsmen.

wordNotes.term: ἀποδώσει (apodōsei) — reward
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to give back or render what is due, used both for reward and for retribution. It is the same verb as “shall give” in verse 8. The phrase “according to his works” repeats the biblical principle of divine judgment by deeds.

verses.bibleText: Of whom be thou ware also; for he hath greatly withstood our words.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Of whom be thou ware also.” Timothy, who will soon travel toward Rome and who ministers in the region where Alexander was known, must be on his guard. The verb means to guard oneself or keep watch against something, and its present tense calls for continual vigilance.

The reason is that Alexander “hath greatly withstood our words.” The verb is the same one used for Jannes and Jambres, who withstood Moses (3:8). “Our words” refers to the message proclaimed by Paul and his companions, and perhaps also to the defense he presented in court. Alexander was not merely a personal enemy; he actively resisted the gospel.

The warning shows that love for the church includes clear-sighted caution. Paul told the Ephesian elders to watch for wolves (Acts 20:29–31), and he here applies the same care to Timothy. Leaving judgment to God (v. 14) does not mean ignoring danger.

wordNotes.term: ἀντέστη τοῖς ἡμετέροις λόγοις (antestē tois hēmeterois logois) — he hath greatly withstood our words
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to set oneself against or resist. The plural “words” points to the content of the message Paul and his co-workers proclaimed. The intensifying adverb shows that Alexander’s opposition was vigorous and deliberate.

verses.bibleText: At my first answer no man stood with me, but all men forsook me: I pray God that it may not be laid to their charge.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“At my first answer no man stood with me.” The word “answer” is the term for a legal defense. Most likely Paul refers to the preliminary hearing in his present trial, a first stage in which the charges were examined before the case proceeded. Some have taken it as a reference to his earlier Roman trial years before, but Timothy would already have known that history, and the context reads naturally as recent news.

In Roman courts a defendant’s friends and patrons would often appear to support him and speak on his behalf. When Paul stood before the tribunal, no one did. “All men forsook me,” he writes, using the same verb he used of Demas (v. 10). Under Nero, association with a man accused of crimes against the state could be deadly, and the Christians of Rome had already suffered savagely. Fear seems to have kept away those who might have stood by him.

Paul’s response mirrors his Lord’s: “I pray God that it may not be laid to their charge.” Jesus prayed for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34), and Stephen prayed with his last breath for those who stoned him (Acts 7:60). Paul treats these frightened believers very differently from Alexander. Alexander had actively opposed the truth; these had failed through weakness, much as the disciples fled when Jesus was arrested (Mark 14:50). The apostle asks God not to reckon their failure against them.

The verse offers a pattern for responding to disappointment in others. Paul does not pretend the desertion did not hurt, yet he refuses to hold it as a grievance. Forgiveness is not denial of the wrong; it is a decision to release the offender to the mercy of God.

wordNotes.term: ἀπολογία (apologia) — answer
wordNotes.explanation: The noun denotes a formal defense, especially in a court of law. Paul uses it of his defense before hostile hearers and of the defense and confirmation of the gospel. Peter uses it for the ready answer every believer should give for the hope within.

wordNotes.term: μὴ αὐτοῖς λογισθείη (mē autois logistheiē) — may it not be laid to their charge
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to reckon or count to someone’s account, the language Paul uses elsewhere for God not counting trespasses against sinners. The optative expresses a prayerful wish, asking God not to enter this failure in the record against them.

verses.bibleText: Notwithstanding the Lord stood with me, and strengthened me; that by me the preaching might be fully known, and that all the Gentiles might hear: and I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Notwithstanding the Lord stood with me, and strengthened me.” The contrast with verse 16 is sharp. Every human supporter was absent, but the Lord was present. The verb means to stand beside someone to help, the posture of an advocate or ally. Christ had stood by Paul before, in the barracks at Jerusalem and on the storm-tossed ship (Acts 23:11; 27:23–24). In the Roman courtroom he did so again. Like Jesus, who said that though his disciples would scatter he was not alone because the Father was with him (John 16:32), Paul discovered that the absence of friends could not leave him truly alone.

The Lord “strengthened” him, literally empowered him, the same word Paul used when he thanked Christ for enabling him for ministry (1 Timothy 1:12) and when he declared that he could do all things through Christ (Philippians 4:13). The strength was given for a purpose: “that by me the preaching might be fully known, and that all the Gentiles might hear.” Paul’s defense became an occasion to proclaim the gospel. The verb “fully known” is the one used in verse 5 for Timothy’s full accomplishment of his ministry. The commission given at his conversion, to bear Christ’s name before Gentiles and kings (Acts 9:15), was fulfilled in the capital of the Gentile world, where representatives of many nations were present.

“And I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion.” The phrase echoes Psalm 22:21, a psalm of the suffering righteous one, and Daniel’s rescue from the lions (Daniel 6:20–22). It is best taken as a vivid figure for deliverance from deadly danger. Paul was not condemned at the first hearing; the case was postponed, giving him time to write this letter. Some have seen in the lion a reference to Nero or to Satan, the roaring lion of 1 Peter 5:8, but the biblical image of rescue from mortal peril fits the context most naturally.

The verse teaches that faithful witness does not depend on human backing. When friends fail, Christ remains, and his strength is sufficient for the testimony he wants given (Matthew 10:18–20).

wordNotes.term: παρέστη (parestē) — stood with me
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to come and stand beside someone, often to help or support them. Paul uses it when asking the Romans to assist Phoebe. Here it describes the Lord taking the place left empty by Paul’s absent friends.

wordNotes.term: ἐρρύσθην ἐκ στόματος λέοντος (errysthēn ek stomatos leontos) — I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to rescue or deliver, and the phrase closely echoes the prayer of Psalm 22:21. It serves as a figure for deliverance from extreme danger, perhaps the threat of immediate condemnation at the first hearing.

verses.bibleText: And the Lord shall deliver me from every evil work, and will preserve me unto his heavenly kingdom: to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
From a past rescue Paul moves to a future certainty. “And the Lord shall deliver me from every evil work.” The wording recalls the petition Jesus taught his disciples, “deliver us from evil” (Matthew 6:13). Paul applies that prayer to himself with full confidence.

The promise must be read alongside verses 6–8. Paul does not expect to be released; he knows he is being poured out. The deliverance he anticipates is therefore not escape from the executioner. It is protection from every hostile design that could destroy his faith, silence his witness, or separate him from Christ. Men may take his life, but no plot of human enemies or of Satan can make him deny his Lord or forfeit the salvation kept for him. Jesus had told his followers not to fear those who can kill the body but cannot destroy the whole person beyond the reach of God (Matthew 10:28).

“And will preserve me unto his heavenly kingdom.” The verb is the ordinary word for “save,” used here with the sense of bringing safely through to a destination. The destination is Christ’s kingdom, called “heavenly” because its origin, character, and King are from heaven. It is the same kingdom named in verse 1, linked with Christ’s appearing. Paul does not describe being carried into that kingdom at the moment of death. He has entrusted his life to the Lord “against that day” (1:12), and he expects the crown “at that day” (v. 8). Between his execution and Christ’s return he will rest in the sleep of death, kept secure by the Lord. When Christ appears, the dead in Christ will be raised incorruptible and enter the kingdom prepared for them (1 Corinthians 15:50–54; Matthew 25:31–34). The preservation Paul speaks of reaches through death to the resurrection.

The thought moves Paul to praise: “to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.” The doxology is directed to “the Lord,” who throughout this passage is Christ (vv. 8, 14, 17). Paul ascribes to Jesus the eternal glory belonging to God (compare 2 Peter 3:18; Revelation 1:5–6). A condemned prisoner, abandoned by friends and facing the sword, ends his account not with complaint but with worship.

wordNotes.term: ῥύσεταί με ὁ κύριος ἀπὸ παντὸς ἔργου πονηροῦ (rhysetai me ho kyrios apo pantos ergou ponērou) — the Lord shall deliver me from every evil work
wordNotes.explanation: The future verb continues the deliverance language of verse 17 and appears to adapt the Lord’s Prayer. “Every evil work” embraces every hostile deed directed against Paul. The promise is not freedom from death but from the power of evil to defeat him finally.

wordNotes.term: σώσει εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν αὐτοῦ τὴν ἐπουράνιον (sōsei eis tēn basileian autou tēn epouranion) — will preserve me unto his heavenly kingdom
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to save or keep safe, and with “into” it describes bringing someone safely to a goal. The kingdom is Christ’s, heavenly in source and nature, and is entered by the redeemed when he comes in glory and raises the dead.

verses.bibleText: Salute Prisca and Aquila, and the household of Onesiphorus.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The closing greetings begin with old friends. “Salute Prisca and Aquila.” Paul first met this Jewish couple in Corinth after they had been expelled from Rome under Claudius. They shared his trade of tentmaking and his home (Acts 18:2–3). They traveled with him to Ephesus, remained there, and helped Apollos understand the way of God more accurately (Acts 18:18–26). A church met in their house (1 Corinthians 16:19), and Paul once said they had risked their own necks for his life (Romans 16:3–4). After a period back in Rome, they are once again in Ephesus, serving alongside Timothy.

Prisca, whom Luke calls by the familiar form Priscilla, is named before her husband in most of the references. The order may reflect the prominence of her service or simply courtesy, and Scripture does not draw a conclusion from it. What is clear is that both husband and wife were valued partners in the gospel.

“And the household of Onesiphorus.” Earlier Paul had prayed for mercy on this family because Onesiphorus had sought him out in Rome and was not ashamed of his chain (1:16–18). Greeting the household rather than the man himself may mean that Onesiphorus was still away from home or that he had died. Paul’s gratitude extends to the whole family that shared in his service.

wordNotes.term: Πρίσκαν καὶ Ἀκύλαν (Priskan kai Akylan) — Prisca and Aquila
wordNotes.explanation: Paul always uses the formal name Prisca, while Acts uses the diminutive Priscilla. The couple appear six times in the New Testament, usually with her named first. They model a household devoted to hospitality, teaching, and missionary partnership.

wordNotes.term: ἄσπασαι (aspasai) — salute
wordNotes.explanation: The imperative of the ordinary verb for greeting someone warmly. Paul uses it frequently at the end of his letters to express affection and to strengthen the bonds between scattered believers. It may be rendered “give my greetings to.”

verses.bibleText: Erastus abode at Corinth: but Trophimus have I left at Miletum sick.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul now accounts for two co-workers who are not with him. “Erastus abode at Corinth.” An Erastus had served with Timothy when Paul sent the two of them ahead into Macedonia (Acts 19:22), and a man of the same name was a city treasurer of Corinth who sent greetings to Rome (Romans 16:23). They may be the same person. The verb “abode” means he stayed behind, which suggests that Paul passed through Corinth on his final journey and that Erastus remained there rather than continuing with him.

“But Trophimus have I left at Miletum sick.” Trophimus was an Ephesian who had traveled with Paul to Jerusalem; his presence with Paul in the city led to the false accusation that the apostle had brought a Gentile into the temple, which set off the riot and Paul’s arrest (Acts 20:4; 21:29). Since Trophimus went on to Jerusalem on that occasion, this mention of leaving him ill at Miletus must refer to a later journey, after Paul’s release from his first Roman imprisonment.

The brief notice carries pastoral weight. The apostle through whom God had worked remarkable healings (Acts 19:11–12; 28:8–9) left a beloved companion behind in sickness. The gift of healing was never a power Paul could use at will. Epaphroditus was near death before God had mercy on him (Philippians 2:26–27), Timothy was given practical counsel for his frequent ailments (1 Timothy 5:23), and Paul himself bore a thorn in the flesh that was not removed (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). Illness among faithful believers is not a sign of weak faith. God sometimes heals, and sometimes gives grace to endure.

wordNotes.term: ἀσθενοῦντα (asthenounta) — sick
wordNotes.explanation: The participle comes from the verb meaning to be weak, used in the New Testament mainly for physical illness. James uses it when directing the sick to call the elders for prayer. Here it explains why Trophimus could not continue traveling with Paul.

wordNotes.term: ἔμεινεν (emeinen) — abode
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to stay or remain in a place. Its use here implies that Erastus did not travel on with Paul, while the companion verb “I left” for Trophimus implies Paul was present when they parted.

verses.bibleText: Do thy diligence to come before winter. Eubulus greeteth thee, and Pudens, and Linus, and Claudia, and all the brethren.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Do thy diligence to come before winter.” Paul repeats the plea of verse 9, now with a deadline. Sailing on the Mediterranean became dangerous after the autumn storms began, and shipping largely ceased from about November until March. Paul had experienced the danger firsthand when his own ship was wrecked after sailing too late in the season (Acts 27:9–12, 20). If Timothy delayed, he might be unable to travel for months, and by spring it might be too late. The cloak requested in verse 13 would be needed then as well. Behind the practical concern lies a deeper one: Paul does not expect his case to wait until the sea lanes reopen.

The greetings that follow come from believers in Rome. “Eubulus greeteth thee, and Pudens, and Linus, and Claudia.” None of these names appears elsewhere in the New Testament. An early tradition identifies Linus as one of the first leaders of the Roman church after the apostles, but beyond that little is known. They were evidently acquainted with Timothy, perhaps from his earlier time in Rome with Paul (Philippians 1:1; Colossians 1:1).

“And all the brethren.” Though no one had stood with Paul at his first defense (v. 16), the Roman believers had not forgotten him or the wider fellowship of the church. Their greeting is a reminder that the body of Christ remained connected across distance and danger. Even in a city where Christians were hunted, believers sent their love to a brother in Ephesus.

The verse balances urgency and community. Paul’s time is short, yet he still notices and names individual believers, giving these otherwise unknown men and women a lasting place in Scripture.

wordNotes.term: πρὸ χειμῶνος (pro cheimōnos) — before winter
wordNotes.explanation: Cheimōn can mean both winter and stormy weather, and the two senses coincide here. Winter closed the seas to most travel. Jesus used the same word when he told his followers to pray that their flight would not be in winter.

wordNotes.term: οἱ ἀδελφοὶ πάντες (hoi adelphoi pantes) — all the brethren
wordNotes.explanation: “Brethren” is the family term for believers who share the same Father through Christ. With “all,” it embraces the whole Christian community in Rome, distinct from Paul’s traveling co-workers, joining in fellowship with Timothy.

verses.bibleText: The Lord Jesus Christ be with thy spirit. Grace be with you. Amen.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The letter ends with a benediction in two parts. “The Lord Jesus Christ be with thy spirit.” Some manuscripts read simply “The Lord,” but the meaning is the same: Christ is the Lord who has been the center of the whole chapter. The pronoun is singular. Paul’s final personal wish for Timothy is that the Lord who stood with him in the courtroom (v. 17) will stand with Timothy in his inner life, in the place where courage and faith are formed. “With thy spirit” is a way of speaking about the whole person in his relationship with God (Galatians 6:18; Philemon 1:25).

“Grace be with you.” The pronoun shifts to the plural. Paul has written to Timothy, but he knows the letter will be read to the congregation in Ephesus, and he extends his blessing to all of them. Every one of Paul’s letters ends with grace, the unearned favor and enabling power of God in Christ that saves, sustains, and equips believers (2 Timothy 1:9; 2:1).

These are the last recorded words of the apostle Paul. They do not focus on himself, his sufferings, or his achievements. They point to the presence of Christ and the grace of God, the resources that would sustain Timothy and the church after Paul’s departure. The work of the gospel would continue because its life never depended on any single servant, however great, but on the Lord who gives grace to all his people.

wordNotes.term: μετὰ τοῦ πνεύματός σου (meta tou pneumatos sou) — with thy spirit
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase appears in several of Paul’s closing benedictions and is equivalent to “with you,” emphasizing the inner life where the Lord’s presence is experienced. The singular pronoun addresses Timothy personally.

wordNotes.term: ἡ χάρις μεθ’ ὑμῶν (hē charis meth’ hymōn) — grace be with you
wordNotes.explanation: The plural pronoun extends the blessing to the whole congregation. Paul closes every letter with grace, the free favor of God in Christ that saves and strengthens. Its brief form here matches the closings of his other late letters.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: If you knew your work was ending, what would you most want to pass on to those who continue it?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: Because Christ will appear as Judge and King, his servants proclaim his word faithfully in every season, endure hardship, and finish their course in the hope of the crown he gives at his coming.
discussionQuestions: How does the coming of Christ as Judge shape the way Timothy is to preach and correct?
What does the phrase “itching ears” reveal about the hearers rather than the teachers?
Why does Paul expect his crown “at that day” rather than at the moment of death?
What do Demas, Mark, and Luke show about faithfulness, failure, and restoration in ministry?
How does Paul’s response to those who deserted him differ from his response to Alexander, and why?
commonMisunderstandings: Preaching “out of season” does not license harshness or tactlessness; the charge requires all longsuffering and careful teaching.
Paul’s confidence in verse 7 is not a boast of self-made merit; his perseverance rested on the grace and strength of the Lord.
Paul does not describe passing into heaven at death; he rests in death and receives his crown with all the faithful at Christ’s appearing.
Deliverance “from every evil work” does not promise escape from execution; it promises that no evil can prevent his safe arrival in Christ’s kingdom.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Hold the charge and the hope together: the ministry of the word is urgent, costly, and patient because it is carried out before the Lord who will appear, judge, and crown his faithful people.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Take up the work entrusted to you, keep to the truth when others drift toward what pleases them, and live as one who loves Christ’s appearing.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: Jesus Christ will visibly appear to judge the living and the dead, raise his sleeping saints, and give the crown of righteousness to all who love his appearing.
flow: Every person will stand before Christ, the righteous Judge, at his appearing.
God’s word calls us to turn from pleasing myths to the truth that saves.
Christ gives his righteousness and strength to those who trust him, enabling them to keep the faith.
Those who die in him rest until he comes; then he raises them and crowns all the faithful together.
To love his appearing is to welcome him now as Lord.
simpleIllustrations: A runner does not receive the wreath at the moment he crosses the line in his own mind; it is placed on him when the judge of the games awards it before everyone.
A ship’s crew loosens the mooring ropes because a voyage lies ahead; Paul spoke of death as a departure because the resurrection morning lay beyond it.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you trust the coming Judge as your Savior now, so that you can love his appearing rather than dread it?
cautions: Do not frighten people with judgment apart from the grace and righteousness Christ freely gives.
Do not suggest that the faithful dead are already crowned; keep the reward at Christ’s appearing.
Do not present Paul’s steadfastness as a standard that people must reach in their own strength.

reflectionQuestions: Am I seeking teachers who tell me what I want to hear, or am I willing to be corrected by the word of God?
Where is the Lord asking me to speak or serve faithfully even though the season feels unfavorable?
What would it mean for me to finish my course, and what is distracting me from it today?
Do I love Christ’s appearing, and how does that hope shape my use of time, money, and friendships?
When others have failed me, am I able to pray that it not be laid to their charge?
